Defense at third is a real liability, the OAA percentile is about as low as it goes, so everything that matters here runs through the bat, and the bat is genuinely loud.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is the strikeout rate sitting against everything else. A 26.7% K% undercuts what is otherwise a genuinely damaging contact shape: 49.0% hard-hit rate, an xSLG of .473 that the projection translates to .515 actual slugging, and 11.5% walks that buy back enough plate appearances to keep the xwOBA at .363. He chases at 34.3%, which is the root cause, and that's the one number the whole offensive profile hangs on — if it doesn't come down, the strikeouts stay elevated and the gap between what his batted-ball quality deserves and what he actually produces stays open. When the sprint speed sits at 29.5 ft/s, though, some of what pitchers get away with on him he simply outruns, and the projection's 37 steals at 700 PA reflects that the speed is genuinely complementary to the power, not a consolation prize for it.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .411 xwOBA at the plate and a 2.72 xERA on the mound, both sitting near the top of the game, and the question isn't whether he's elite but whether the Dodgers ever let him pitch enough to matter. The bat is built on contact quality: 93.7 mph average exit velo, a 16.8% barrel rate, and 14.0% walks doing the heavy lifting while a 22.8% strikeout rate stays manageable enough not to eat into the value. On the mound, a 30.4% whiff rate pairs with 98.1 mph on the fastball and a xwOBA against of .257, which is ace-caliber contact suppression even if the chase rate at 30.0% leaves a little out there. The projection lands at .285/.391/.545 with 37 home runs across 688 plate appearances, and the whole profile hinges on workload: if Los Angeles treats him primarily as a DH, you're leaving the 2.72 xERA version on the shelf, which is its own kind of waste.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact tool is elite, the swing-and-miss is the gap. At 94.3 mph average exit velocity, De La Cruz sits at the 99th percentile in raw power application, and a 14.9% barrel rate with 52.8% hard contact explains why his xwOBA of .369 and xSLG of .491 both land in the upper tier — the projection's .492 SLG is just the Statcast profile translated to a full season. The problem is a 28.1% whiff rate that keeps his K% at 27.3%, and until that comes down, every hot streak carries a correction waiting behind it. If the strikeout rate softens even modestly, you have a 27-homer, 33-steal shortstop posting an .842 OPS who can hurt you six different ways; if it doesn't, he's still producing, just with more variance than the raw tools deserve.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The gap between a .349 xwOBA and an 11.1% barrel rate, on a guy with a 36.9% chase rate, is the whole tension in this profile. Abrams is squaring the ball up at a rate his raw contact numbers don't fully explain, which is why the projection lands at .521 SLG despite exit velocity that grades just a tick above the middle of the league. The chase number is the lever: if it stays where it is, the strikeouts hold at 21.6% and the power plays, but a disciplinary slide erodes the xwOBA gains faster than the raw tools can compensate. At 25, with 28 projected steals and a shortstop's frame, the upside is a middle-of-the-order catalyst, and the floor is a high-variance regular whose value lives and dies by plate coverage.

reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact profile is a paradox: a 93.2 mph average exit velocity and a 13.6% barrel rate sitting alongside a 35.2% chase rate and a 30.6% whiff rate. Walker can absolutely wreck a fastball he recognizes, and he does it often enough that the underlying numbers (.360 xwOBA, .491 xSLG) are genuinely impressive for a 24-year-old. The whole profile hinges on whether the plate discipline firms up enough to keep pitchers from just burying breaking balls and watching him expand, because the strikeout rate is the ceiling suppressor, not the power. If the chase rate trends toward league average, the projection (.272/.334/.477 with 30 home runs in 672 plate appearances) becomes a floor; if it stays at 35.2%, he's a streaky middle-of-the-order bat you can game-plan against.

reports.name: Logan Gilbert
reports.published_report: The walk rate tells you almost everything: 5.4% BB%, sitting at the 92nd percentile, means he beats himself almost never. Pair that with a 29.9% whiff rate and a 33.5% chase rate and you have a starter who wins with control and deception rather than pure swing-and-miss venom. The barrel exposure is a real thing, a 10.0% barrel rate in the 15th percentile, suggesting hitters do damage when they connect. But his contact management has been good enough that a 3.64 xERA and 184.7 projected innings hold up, and the profile hinges entirely on that BB% staying low. If he loses the strike-throwing edge, the modest hard-contact suppression has nowhere to hide, and he slides from solid number-two territory into a back-end innings eater.

reports.name: Carson Benge
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .277 against a projected .259 AVG, which tells you the contact quality is outrunning what's showing up in the box score — and the 85th-percentile read on expected batting average is the loudest thing in his Statcast profile. His raw power is ordinary, 89.1 mph exit velocity at the 45th percentile, barrel rate squarely league-average, which means the projection's 16 home runs and .392 SLG lean on sustained contact volume rather than thump. What keeps this profile interesting is 28.5 ft/s sprint speed, 83rd percentile, which makes the 22 projected steals credible and covers for a walk rate sitting at just 7.4%. If the .337 xwOBA translates and the speed stays healthy, he's a genuine everyday outfielder, the kind who doesn't profile in any one tool but doesn't give the lineup a dead spot either; if the walks don't grow and the contact luck normalizes downward, you're left with a useful fourth outfielder who steals a bag.

reports.name: Mason Miller
reports.published_report: A 49.4% strikeout rate with a 48.0% whiff rate tells you what he is before you even get to the ERA. Miller's xERA sits at 1.32 and his xwOBA against is .176, and those figures aren't being propped up by soft contact luck — hitters are averaging 85.1 mph off the bat, barrels are at 2.8%, and a 38.0% chase rate explains how he keeps getting to two strikes in the first place. The one real exposure is the 8.7% walk rate, which sits near the middle of the league and is the only reason the profile carries any tension at all; if that number climbs, the margin for error against a thin projection of 67.9 innings shrinks fast. With 39 saves projected and a 1.23 ERA to go with it, he looks like the best version of what a closer can actually be right now.

reports.name: Jonathan Aranda
reports.published_report: The .357 xwOBA is the argument: a contact profile built on an 11.7% walk rate and 91.0 mph average exit velocity that together pull his expected production well above what a 23.5% strikeout rate would usually allow. The swing decisions are genuinely good, a 28.8% chase rate that sits comfortably below the league median, and a 21.5% whiff rate that explains why the walks translate into actual damage rather than just patience theater. The projection reads .276/.368/.432 across a full 686 PA, and the Statcast profile earns that line: the xSLG of .451 suggests the .432 SLG has room to breathe rather than regress. The one honest dependency is playing time, because Tampa has organizational depth at first, and if Aranda doesn't get those 686 PA, you're looking at a very good part-time bat instead of a legitimate everyday first baseman.

reports.name: Drew Rasmussen
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole profile in one number: 4.3% puts him in the 97th percentile, and almost everything downstream flows from it. Rasmussen doesn't miss as many bats as you'd want from a front-line arm, but a 34.0% chase rate gets hitters to expand, and when they do make contact, a 32.8% hard-hit rate and .275 xwOBA say the damage stays manageable. The projection's 3.26 ERA over 168.4 innings looks earned given a 3.12 xERA — the shape of the profile supports the workload, the command does too. The dependency is health; if he stays on the mound, this is a mid-rotation starter who beats you with plus command and reasonable contact suppression, and if he doesn't, there's not enough swing-and-miss (24.8% whiff rate) to survive shortened outings against better lineups.

The Statcast profile says a hitter who squares the ball up at an 82nd-percentile clip but runs a below-average chase rate and middling hard-hit percentage, which is how you get real power from a guy who isn't an elite contact machine. The .436 projected SLG drags behind the .460 xSLG because the projection is discounting some of that barrel production, and if he keeps barreling at his current rate across a full 666-PA season, the 24 projected home runs could be a floor. The profile hinges on that barrel rate holding, because without it you're left with average contact quality, a .247 average, and a .757 OPS that profiles as a solid but replaceable corner outfielder.

Basallo's 91.3 mph average exit velocity and 12.9% barrel rate sit in the same neighborhood, both translating to an .469 xSLG that says 25 home runs in 493 projected plate appearances is a reasonable expectation, not an optimistic one. But a 40.2% chase rate and 31.6% whiff rate are the kind of numbers that let big-league pitching dictate the at-bat, and the .250 xBA tells you hits aren't hiding in the contact profile waiting to emerge. If the chase rate doesn't come down, you're looking at a plus-power bat that spends most of his time in the bottom third of the lineup, a second-division regular who makes pitchers comfortable.

reports.name: Ryan Weathers
reports.published_report: The ERA-versus-xERA split is the whole argument here. Weathers is projecting at 3.88 ERA across 153.7 innings, but the Statcast profile puts his xERA at 4.37, and the underlying contact story backs that skepticism: a 42.5% hard-hit rate with a 9.1% barrel rate against him tells you hitters are making real contact when they connect. The redeeming piece is the command-and-miss combination, a 26.1% strikeout rate sitting alongside a 6.8% walk rate, which keeps him functional even when the ball gets hit hard. If the ERA and xERA close the gap in the wrong direction, he's a back-end starter on a short leash; if the strikeout and walk rates hold and the contact profile softens even modestly, the 153.7-inning workload becomes believable as a mid-rotation contributor for New York.

reports.name: MacKenzie Gore
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is doing most of the heavy lifting here. Gore's Statcast profile is a study in mismatched signals: a 26.0% K% that sits comfortably above average, a 3.83 xERA that flatters the actual numbers, and then a barrel rate and hard-hit rate that land in the bottom quarter of the league, which doesn't square with a 4.45 ERA projection over 178.9 innings. The walk rate at 8.4% is the friction point, sitting right at average and keeping him from converting that strikeout upside into cleaner results. If the command tightens and the contact-quality numbers stabilize toward what the xERA suggests, he's a mid-rotation piece who eats innings and misses bats; if the walks stay and the hard contact catches up to the barrel rate, the projection ERA is probably the floor.

reports.name: Dustin May
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a contradiction wrapped in a fastball. May's 96.9 mph heater and 2328 rpm spin are legitimate weapons, and his 6.5% barrel rate suggests he's doing something right at the top of the zone, but a 46.1% hard-hit rate and 90.1 mph average exit velocity tell you that when hitters do make contact, they're squaring it up regularly. His 22.4% whiff rate sits in the bottom quarter of starters, which is the core problem: the velocity and spin aren't generating enough swing-and-miss to suppress damage from that contact. The projection at 4.29 ERA over 165.6 innings with a 1.30 WHIP is roughly what you get when a mid-rotation arm has one elite tool and no reliable secondary to hide behind, a back-end regular who keeps a rotation spot if the stuff plays up but becomes an innings-eating liability if the contact profile stays this loud.

reports.name: Rafael Devers
reports.published_report: The contact metrics are a problem. Devers hits the ball as hard as almost anyone, 92.3 mph average exit velocity and a 50.2% hard-hit rate that both land in the 90th-percentile range, but a 29.1% whiff rate undercuts the whole thing, pulling his xBA down to .233 and creating a real gap between the raw power and what he actually puts on the board. The .451 xSLG is honest, the 31 projected home runs are believable, and then you look at the .246 projected average and understand exactly where the ceiling went. Everything here hinges on whether he can tighten the zone enough to let the exit velocity do its job; if the whiff rate holds, you have a .793 OPS slugger with a strikeout problem and a floor that isn't pretty.

reports.name: Theo Gillen
reports.published_report: The .429 OBP and 36 stolen bases across AA & A+ are loud, but the whole argument rests on whether a 20-year-old left-handed hitter with a .393 BABIP is making real contact or riding luck. Translated to the majors, his strikeout rate lands at 25.5% against a pool where 22.0% is average, and his ISO shrinks from .251 to .168, which is above the MLB mean but not the power profile the raw slash line implies. The plate discipline holds up better in translation, a 10.7% walk rate against a league figure of 8.5%, and 54 walks across 382 PA is a real skill at any level. If the BABIP normalizes and the strikeouts climb, what's left is a useful bench piece with speed and a decent eye; if the bat-to-ball is genuine and the contact quality travels, he's a platoon contributor with legitimate on-base value, which is the ceiling this profile points toward in one to two years.

What the profile leans on is chase rate, 32.7%, because the whiff rate at 25.9% is roughly league-average, meaning he's generating strikeouts more by expanding the zone than by blowing hitters away inside it; if that chase rate regresses, the strikeout number follows and so does everything else. reports.name: Caleb Durbin
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is almost entirely bottom-decile: 84.0 mph average exit velocity, a 2.4% barrel rate, 27.0% hard-hit rate. What saves Durbin as a viable regular is that he almost never swings and misses, posting a 15.2% whiff rate that grades in the 92nd percentile, which keeps him in counts long enough to make weak contact work and holds his K% down to 13.9%. The projection leans on that skill translating across a full 561 PA season, producing a .247/.315/.396 line with 19 steals as the speed underwriting what the bat can't quite provide. Keaschall's chase rate sits at 22.5% and his strikeout rate at 15.1%, both comfortably better than league average, which is how a 23-year-old earns 563 projected plate appearances as a big-leaguer. But his average exit velocity is 84.8 mph and his barrel rate is 2.8%, and those numbers explain why a .300 xwOBA and a projected .349 SLG land where they do, leaving OPS at .697. The 19 projected steals at second base add a dimension the bat alone can't, and if the discipline holds while the contact quality creeps up even modestly, he's a usable everyday player; if it doesn't, you're looking at a fast, patient hitter with nothing behind the count to make pitchers uncomfortable.

reports.name: Christian Scott
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the carry piece here, and the walk rate is the weight dragging against it. Christian Scott punches out 28.8% of hitters he faces, a number that lives in the top tier of starters, but his 10.2 BB% sits near the bottom of the league, and that gap is the whole profile. The contact metrics are quietly interesting: a 34.3% hard-hit rate sounds alarming until you see the 87.6 mph average exit velocity and 6.3% barrel rate sitting comfortably above league norms, suggesting the damage is dispersed rather than concentrated. A 3.75 xERA against a 3.33 projected ERA tells you the projection leans on sequencing holding up, and if the walks stay where they are, that lean gets uncomfortable fast. Bring the BB% down toward league average and this is a genuine mid-rotation starter; leave it at 10.2% and the strikeouts are just barely covering the mess.

reports.name: Kahlil Watson
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the engine here. Watson is drawing 40 walks in 284 AAA plate appearances this season, a 14% clip that translates to 11.1% against big-league pitching, comfortably ahead of what most MLB hitters manage. The power is doing its job too — 12 home runs and a .215 ISO at AAA, which softens to .163 in translation, just above the MLB mean. The problem is the 83 strikeouts, a 29% rate at AAA that translates to 27.6% in the majors, and that's the hinge: if the contact rate doesn't tighten, the walks and the pop get buried under the swing-and-miss, and what's left is a bench or depth piece who runs well but can't stay in a lineup long enough to matter. If the bat-to-ball improves even modestly, the combination of patience, power, and 17 stolen bases makes a genuine platoon case.

reports.name: Kumar Rocker
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 4.58 and the hard-hit rate is 42.1%, and those two numbers tell you most of what you need to know about where Rocker actually stands. His chase rate at 31.7% is genuinely useful, and whiff rate at 25.6% is league-average, but the strikeout rate is only 21.3%, meaning he's generating enough weak contact to avoid disaster in stretches, not consistently missing bats. The fastball spin at 2153 rpm is the quiet problem: without carry or deception at that spin grade, 94.4 mph plays smaller than it looks on a radar gun, and hitters are squaring him up at a rate that keeps the xwOBA at .329. If the projection's 4.10 ERA looks friendlier than the Statcast picture, that's exactly the gap to watch, because he can hold a rotation spot at 152.4 projected innings, but the profile right now is a back-end starter whose margin for error depends on keeping the walk rate near 8.7% and hoping the contact suppression catches up to the batted-ball outcomes.

reports.name: Orion Kerkering
reports.published_report: The contact-suppression numbers here are genuinely striking: a 26.6% hard-hit rate and 84.8 mph average exit velocity that both sit near the top of the league, and an xwOBA of .273 and xERA of 3.07 that confirm hitters are doing nothing with what he gives them. The problem is obvious and it's the whole tension in the profile: a 13.3% walk rate that grades out in the bottom tier of the league cancels much of that contact quality, because a reliever who can't find the zone is always one bad stretch from imploding. His 97.5 mph fastball gives him the stuff to be a reliable high-leverage piece in Philadelphia's pen, and the projected 2.98 ERA across 62.6 innings reflects what happens when the command holds together. If the walk rate doesn't come down, he stays exactly what he is now: a guy who misses barrels but beats himself.

reports.name: Alex Bregman

The projection's .341 OBP is built on that elite discipline, and an 11.1% walk rate backed by a chase rate that good has a shape that holds, but the .391 SLG tells you the power simply isn't there to punish the walks downstream — 18 home runs across 707 plate appearances is a contact-first corner bat without the contact quality you'd want at the position. reports.name: Michael Lombardi
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud, the walk rate is a problem, and they're both real. Lombardi is punching out batters at 12.6 per nine across 72 innings at A-ball in 2026, which translates to roughly 8.4 K/9 in MLB context, nearly identical to the MLB mean, but his 44 walks in that same stretch translate to 5.5 BB/9 where MLB starters average 3.2. The K-BB% at 18% looks fine among A-ball peers, but the MLB-equivalent drops it to 11.1% against a field where 13.5% is the baseline. If the command tightens over the next two or three years, there's a back-end arm here; if it doesn't, what's left is a depth piece.

reports.name: Jim Jarvis
reports.published_report:
The contact-first shortstop profile is the whole argument here, and the power is what keeps the ceiling in check. Jim Jarvis is hitting .313 at AAA with 46 walks against 55 strikeouts in 348 plate appearances, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout rate at 18.9% in a league that runs 22.0%, his walk rate at 10.8% where the field sits at 8.5%. The 32 stolen bases are loud. But six home runs and a .148 ISO at AAA translate to .13 against MLB pitching, and nothing in the shape of this profile suggests that gap narrows.

If the bat-to-ball and speed carry over, he's a low-end everyday shortstop; if a big league defense solves him, he's a reserve.

reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.
